beginner.headline: Women Speak Up About Problems in Television
beginner.brief: Recent news stories raise questions about how powerful people in television treat others. These stories follow changes that began years ago. Reporters started looking into these stories years ago. Their work can take a long time. Kirsty Wark says more women speak up because they see other women doing this. Freeman says women now feel that people will listen to them. A workers' group says some television workers are still afraid to report problems. Lucy Beaumont says some well-known people stay quiet because they fear losing work. A meeting with television leaders is planned for next week to discuss keeping people safe. People who run television companies also need to help stop people from hurting others.

intermediate.headline: Entertainment Abuse Stories Reflect Years of Change
intermediate.brief: Recent abuse stories in entertainment reflect the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural change. The television programme Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on the programme deny all the allegations. The recent stories began with journalistic investigations that started years ago. Investigations usually take a long time because journalists gather evidence, check information and ask people to respond. According to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, seeing other women come forward has given more women the courage to share their experiences. In the past, women feared retaliation, meaning harmful action against them for reporting abuse. Unions say junior freelance workers, who often have an uncertain income, still find it difficult to report problems. Even well-known people may fear that raising concerns will cost them work, comedian Lucy Beaumont said. Social media has also helped encourage people to report their experiences. Harriet Wistrich from the Centre for Women's Justice says wealthy or famous people often use legal measures to discourage reporting. There is growing recognition that leaders of media organisations have a responsibility to address abuse, rather than leaving victims to act alone. Philippa Childs says the creative industries' current internal reporting systems are inadequate, meaning they do not work well enough.

advanced.headline: Entertainment's Reckoning and the Limits of Cultural Change
advanced.brief: Recent entertainment scandals may look like a sudden reckoning, but the article argues that they reflect changes set in motion years earlier. The revelations emerged from journalistic inquiries that had been under way for years. Such inquiries typically proceed through an initial tip-off, evidence-gathering, corroboration and requests for responses before publication. The article reports that entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault. It also reports that Married at First Sight UK was cancelled following rape allegations involving the programme. Walliams and the men accused on Married at First Sight UK deny the allegations against them. The article traces much of the impetus for women to disclose their experiences to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement. Seeing action taken can encourage further disclosures by challenging the assumption that reporting abuse achieves nothing. Unions say that precarious incomes can nevertheless make it difficult for junior freelance workers to raise concerns. Harriet Wistrich of the Centre for Women's Justice says wealthy or famous people often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from speaking out. A High Court judge rejected Walliams's request for an injunction to prevent him from being named. According to the article, ministers have criticised non-disclosure agreements and called for tighter restrictions on their use. The article reports that a review found no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised. What is increasingly recognised is that senior media executives must help root out abuse, rather than leaving the burden entirely with victims. Philippa Childs argues that existing internal reporting mechanisms do not adequately serve their purpose. Wark warns that abuse cannot be dismissed as a legacy of an earlier era and calls for changes within the industry today. The article ends by asking whether these events could mark a watershed moment for the industry.
